title: Applying an interior lime render finish coat
subtitle: Mix and apply a thin lime putty top coat to a scratch-coated interior wall
excerpt: How to apply a lime putty finish coat to an interior wall. Covers mixing lime putty with fine aggregate, applying it with a trowel to a prepared scratch coat, and finishing with a float and brush.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1880s, public domain). UK Lime Centre technical guidance (open access). Traditional lime plastering practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Calcium hydroxide paste produced by slaking quicklime in excess water and leaving it to mature. Mature lime putty is smooth, plastic, and ready to use. It carbonates slowly on exposure to air, hardening back to calcium carbonate. A more workable binder than hydraulic lime for fine finish coats.

The first render coat applied to a wall surface. It is scratched (scored) with a comb scratcher before it sets to provide a mechanical key for the subsequent finish coat. Also called the floating coat.

The slow hardening process by which lime absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and reverts to calcium carbonate. Carbonation requires moisture and air movement. A thick lime finish coat can take weeks to harden fully.

content.text: A lime render finish coat is a thin top coat of
lime putty
and fine aggregate applied to a prepared
scratch coat
. The finish hardens slowly by
carbonation
and gives period walls a breathable, slightly textured surface that takes limewash or mineral paint. The correct technique is light pressure and patience: lime putty will not be hurried.

attrs.title: Protective equipment
attrs.body: Lime is strongly alkaline. Wear chemical-resistant gloves throughout and goggles when mixing. Lime dust irritates the eyes and airways; work in a ventilated space.

content.text: Prepare the scratch coat

The scratch coat must be at least three to four weeks old and dry before applying the finish coat. Dampen the scratch coat with clean water using a brush 30 minutes before you start. Lime finish bonds to a slightly damp surface; it will not bond to a dust-dry or waterlogged one. Check the scratch coat surface by pressing a fingernail in: it should feel firm but not leave a mark. Knock off any sharp ridges left by the scratch tool.
Mix the finish coat

A standard lime putty finish coat uses 1 part mature lime putty to 1.5 to 2 parts washed fine sharp sand or marble dust by volume. Mix thoroughly in a dedicated plastic bucket until the colour is even and the mix has the consistency of thick Greek yoghurt. Do not add water; the lime putty already contains the correct amount. If the mix feels stiff, work it with the trowel for another five minutes before adding anything.
Apply the first pass

Load the hawk with a modest amount of mix, no more than what you can apply in 10 minutes. Apply the lime render to the wall with the plasterers trowel, working in arcing sweeps from the hawk in 3 to 4 mm layers. The goal is a consistent thickness across the surface, not a polished finish at this pass. Work from the top of the wall down and keep a wet edge. If a section begins to stiffen before you can return to it, dampen it lightly with a brush before picking up from that point.
Float and close the surface

When the first pass has firmed slightly (roughly 30 to 60 minutes depending on temperature and humidity), work over the surface with a plastic float in tight circular movements. This presses the fine aggregate in and closes the larger open pores. The surface should show a fine, slightly open texture when floated: not a mirror, not a rough scratch coat. If the float tears the surface, the plaster is too wet; wait another 15 minutes and try again.
Damp the surface and allow to cure

Lime finish coat must cure slowly. Mist the surface with water two or three times a day for the first week. In warm or windy conditions, hang a damp cloth or polythene sheet a few centimetres from the wall to retain moisture. Do not allow the surface to dry out rapidly, especially in summer. Full hardness by carbonation takes several weeks; the wall is ready to limewash or paint once the surface shows no dark damp patches and feels hard to the fingernail.
Variations

For a polished lime finish, add a second very thin pass of lime putty only (no aggregate) once the floated coat has firmed, and close it with the steel trowel in tight circular strokes. This gives a smoother finish that still breathes.

Natural pigment powders mixed into the lime putty before application give a through-colour finish that does not peel or flake. Use pigments designed for lime; ordinary paint pigments may react with the alkaline binder.
On listed buildings where exact texture matching is required, sample the original plaster before ordering aggregate. Buff sand, silver sand, and crushed limestone give different surface characters.

attrs.symptom: Finish coat pulls away from the scratch coat
attrs.cause: The scratch coat was too dry when the finish was applied, or the scratch coat surface was not dampened.
attrs.fix: Remove the failing area, remoisten the scratch coat, and re-apply. Do not skip the pre-damping step.

attrs.symptom: Surface cracks in a fine map pattern as it dries
attrs.cause: Too much lime putty relative to aggregate, or the coat was applied too thick in one pass.
attrs.fix: Map cracking on a thin coat is normal and usually closes as the lime carbonates. Deep or wide cracks indicate too-lean a mix; float back in with fresh mix.

attrs.symptom: Surface stays soft and powdery after several weeks
attrs.cause: Poor ventilation or very high humidity has prevented carbonation. Lime needs air movement and CO2 to harden.
attrs.fix: Ventilate the room thoroughly for several days. In severe cases in a sealed basement or vault, a small amount of hydraulic lime in the mix accelerates initial set.
